PGP 2025-27, Indian Institute of Management Indore | vikram.rathore@iimidr.ac.in

- Sports Secretary, Officers' Mess, 2021-22

transcript.text: Hi Vikram, thanks for making the time. I'm on the team hiring for this role. Over the next 15 minutes or so I'd like to go into your experience, and you'll have time for questions at the end. What topic from your MBA courses have you found most interesting recently?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: Um sure sir thank you for the question so actually one topic I have found really interesting is supply chain optimization particularly the models around inventory management like EOQ and just-in-time practices so in one of our core courses we did a live case with a beverage distributor where we had to redesign their reorder policies I liked working out the calculations but also understanding the assumptions like lead times and demand variability so this connected a lot with my summer internship at Tata Steel as well where I tried to apply some of these concepts while building the spares stocking model so I feel these frameworks are very practical and link theory to real-world decisions
Thanks. Walk me through your career so far, from the Army through your MBA and summer internship.
transcript.why: I asked this to understand which part of your MBA experience has interested you recently and to begin the interview.

transcript.text: Sure sir so I started my career after engineering by joining the Indian Army specifically the Corps of EME as a Lieutenant in 2017 so my first role was officer-in-charge of a training cadre where I was responsible for a batch of 40 craftsmen and mainly oversaw their technical upskilling and assessment then after a year I got promoted to Captain and was posted to Rajasthan where I was commanding a 120-member Light Repair Workshop we provided technical support to an armoured regiment and here my main responsibility was ensuring high availability of their fleet so one challenge was that our average vehicle turnaround time for repairs was quite high like 9 days so I tried to streamline the spares indent procedure and actually set up a forward spares cell near the frontline which helped us bring the turnaround time down to 5 days I also managed an inventory worth around 14 crore across 3 different depots and during two consecutive annual audits our team brought discrepancies to zero which was not the norm before apart from day-to-day operations I handled crisis situations as well like during a flash flood exercise in Barmer I took charge of the recovery ops and we managed to recover 22 stranded vehicles with no casualties after five years in the Army I decided to shift towards the private sector so I spent two years preparing for CAT and also volunteered as an instructor at a veterans’ skilling centre in Jaipur mainly teaching basic computer skills to ex-servicemen then I joined IIM Indore in 2025 where I have maintained a 7.4 CGPA so far and got involved in academic and extracurricular clubs during the summer I interned at Tata Steel in their Kalinganagar plant as an operations intern my main project was to build a criticality-based spares stocking model for their hot strip mill so by classifying spares based on criticality and analysing usage patterns I projected a possible INR 3.2 crore reduction in inventory holding without increasing breakdown risk I also mapped the whole repair process across four departments and proposed a single work-order queue which the cold rolling mill later agreed to pilot I was given a PPI at the end so that’s been my career journey so far sir
You mentioned classifying 312 hot strip mill spares and projecting a reduction in inventory holding. What problem were you trying to solve with that model?
transcript.why: You described the Tata Steel spares model in your overview, so I asked about the specific business problem behind it rather than asking you to retell the entire internship.

transcript.text: Yeah so basically the core problem was that the spares inventory in the hot strip mill was quite bloated and there was a lot of capital locked up in parts that were hardly ever used at the same time there was a big fear from the maintenance team that if we reduced stocking levels arbitrarily we'd increase the risk of unplanned breakdowns or higher downtime so it was a balancing act between cost efficiency and operational reliability actually my mentor at Tata Steel told me that they had been questioned in a recent audit about why their spares inventory holding cost was above the target benchmark so my job was to build a framework that would identify which spares could safely have their stocking levels reduced and which ones were absolutely critical and needed to be always available so first I classified the 312 spares according to their criticality to plant operations like for example a failure of certain gearboxes would cause a full line stoppage whereas some bolts or covers were never critical I checked past breakdown logs checked lead times for procurement and spoke with maintenance heads to rank these items I then proposed revised minimum and maximum stock levels for each class and ran scenarios to check for potential stockouts based on past consumption that’s how I projected a 3.2 crore reduction in holding cost without increasing breakdown risk basically by shifting from a flat stocking policy to a differentiated one
You projected INR 3.2 crore in savings. What was that figure compared against?
transcript.why: You explained how you classified the spares and set revised stock levels, so I asked how the projected INR 3.2 crore reduction was established and compared.

transcript.text: So sir actually the 3.2 crore figure was the projected reduction in inventory value compared to the opening balance of spares inventory in the hot strip mill at the start of my project basically when I joined I asked the stores and finance team for the current total value of all 312 stocked spares and then after doing the criticality-based classification and calculating revised min-max levels I did a simulation using past issuance data and calculated how much inventory value would be locked in if these new stocking norms were followed so the difference between the existing inventory and the projected one under my model gave me the 3.2 crore number so it’s not just annual savings it’s the potential one-time reduction in working capital if they implemented my recommendations and brought down excess inventory
Looking back at that analysis, what would you do differently now?
transcript.why: You explained how the projected reduction was calculated and what it represented. I asked what you would change now to understand how you reflect on the analysis and its limitations.

transcript.text: Um actually looking back I think one area where I would do things differently is I’d focus more on implementation challenges rather than only the theoretical model so at that time I spent a lot of effort on classifying the spares and simulating stock levels but later on I realized that convincing the maintenance and procurement teams to actually change their stocking practices is not so simple for example I should have involved end users more from the initial stage because after presenting my findings some of the supervisors raised concerns about data gaps like for certain spares the usage info was incomplete or not digitized also if I were to redo it I’d probably conduct more pilot trials for a small group of critical spares first instead of suggesting a plant-wide rollout that way the teams could see the practical benefits without feeling too much risk I’d also look to integrate dynamic demand forecasting maybe using a simple tool like Excel-based moving averages because I’ve since learned in class that fixed min-max levels can miss seasonal or campaign-based spikes so overall I’d spend more time on stakeholder buy-in and monitoring constraints in implementation not just the analytics side
Let’s move to your Army experience. What was the hardest part of commanding the 120-member repair workshop in Rajasthan?
transcript.why: You explained what you would change in the analysis, including involving users earlier and piloting the recommendations before wider rollout. I’m moving to a leadership example from your Army experience.

transcript.text: Yes sir so I think honestly for me the hardest part was managing people from such diverse backgrounds and maintaining motivation and discipline during long stretches of routine work actually unlike combat units we were mostly in a technical support role which meant our daily tasks like preventive maintenance or routine repairs could become quite repetitive but our output directly impacted the operational readiness of the armoured regiment so keeping the team alert and focused was challenging especially in the Rajasthan climate which gets really harsh in summer I remember when there were urgent requirements like before a major exercise or during field deployments everyone’s motivation was automatically high but in peacetime or between exercises a sense of complacency could set in so what I learned was that I couldn’t just rely on orders I had to be more involved at the ground level so I started doing more frequent informal check-ins with my junior supervisors and also rotated tricky tasks among different teams to prevent boredom I also tried starting some small recognition practices like calling out top performers in the daily roll call and that surprisingly boosted morale another tough part was resource constraints sometimes we didn’t get enough spares on time but I had to balance the seniors’ expectations with my team’s realities so overall, I’d say the biggest challenge was sustaining high morale and discipline in a tough environment without always having big triggers like crisis situations and learning to adapt my leadership style accordingly
When you noticed complacency between exercises, what did you personally change first in the workshop’s routine?
transcript.why: You described several leadership practices, but not a specific instance showing what changed because of them. I asked for the first decision you made so the example can be tied to a concrete event.

transcript.text: Um yeah so the first thing I personally changed was increasing my own presence on the shop floor during those quieter periods like earlier I used to mostly rely on my section heads for updates but once I noticed the drop in energy and small lapses in work quality I started spending more time physically with different teams especially in the engine overhaul and electrical repair bays I’d join the morning briefings and sometimes even small tool checks just to show that their daily work was being noticed and valued also I tried to mix up the task allocation instead of the same people always getting routine checks I began rotating roles so for instance someone who usually did only inspection might get a chance to assist on a major recovery task under supervision this made things less monotonous and gave younger craftsmen a sense that they were being trusted with higher responsibility plus I introduced short weekly skill challenges for the whole platoon like timed breakdown drills and the winners got small privileges like a day’s lighter duty or leading a team for the next repair so these were simple changes but I think starting with my own involvement and then making the routine less predictable helped reduce that complacency and improved both morale and attention to detail

topics.question: Let’s turn to an inventory decision. How would you set a stocking policy for a critical spare with intermittent demand and a high cost of downtime?
answer_plan: Define the spare’s criticality, downtime cost, lead time, repair options, and available substitutes.
Estimate the required service level and compare shortage cost with holding, obsolescence, and emergency-order cost.
Set the reorder point and safety stock from the demand and lead-time evidence rather than defaulting to one unit.
State when the policy should be reviewed or replaced by emergency procurement, pooling, or supplier-held stock.
topics.example_answer: I would first define the required service level by comparing the cost of downtime with the cost of holding or urgently procuring the spare. Then I would examine intermittent demand, supplier lead time, repair options, substitutes, obsolescence risk, and whether the asset has redundancy. For a highly critical item with long or uncertain lead time, I would hold safety stock or arrange supplier-held stock. I would avoid a fixed one-unit rule when the part is expensive, perishable, obsolete quickly, or available reliably at short notice.

ratings.label: Accuracy
ratings.reason: You correctly considered criticality, lead time, downtime cost, substitutes, and carrying cost, but treating one unit as a default is too broad without a defined service target or review rule.
ratings.quote: I’d recommend always having at least one unit in stock

ratings.label: Depth and reasoning
ratings.reason: You explained the availability-versus-cost trade-off and named several conditions that change the policy.
ratings.quote: obsolescence, shelf life, cost, or logistics become dominant concerns

ratings.label: Real example
ratings.reason: You connected the approach to your Tata Steel analysis of historical data and critical spares.
ratings.quote: what I did in Tata Steel was to analyse historical data

ratings.label: Handling follow-ups
ratings.reason: You directly listed situations where the one-unit rule would be unsuitable and explained why each matters.
ratings.quote: the lead time for procurement is genuinely very short and reliable

follow_ups.question: You proposed keeping at least one unit available. When would that stocking policy be unsuitable for the spare?
follow_ups.why: You explained why a critical spare may justify extra stock, but not when keeping one unit as a minimum would be unsuitable. I asked for the trade-off behind that decision.

topics.went_well: You made the key trade-off explicit instead of choosing inventory purely from average demand.
topics.went_well_quote: I’d also calculate the expected lost sales or downtime cost and compare that with the carrying cost
topics.to_fix: The policy sounded too fixed for intermittent demand. The answer needed a clearer decision sequence using demand uncertainty, lead time, service level, substitutes, and the cost of excess stock.
topics.to_fix_quote: keep minimum one unit always available
